rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Joint CEE/MAE Distinguished Seminar Abstract: This talk will discuss two peculiar effects we recently discovered: the photomolecular effect and the evaporative refrigeration effect. To explain super-thermal solar-interfacial evaporation from hydrogels and other porous materials, we hypothesize that photons can directly cleave off water clusters at the liquid-vapor interface in a way similar to the photoelectric effect, which we call the photomolecular effect. I will discuss experimental evidence we have so far. This photomolecular evaporation process may exist widely in nature. Our studies on photomolecular evaporation also led us to investigate peculiarities in thermal evaporation. At an evaporating interface, a temperature discontinuity exists between the liquid and the vapor sides, which was predicted by theories and observed in some experiments. However, the existing theories cannot explain experiments. We develop a new interfacial condition that can be used to couple transport on both sides of the interface, leading to agreements between theory and experiments. Our modeling reveals the existence of a new refrigeration effect: the vapor temperature can drop below that of the liquid film and in fact, lower than even the condensing surface temperature. This effect has yet to be confirmed experimentally and may find applications in air-conditioning and refrigeration. Biography: Gang Chen is the Carl Richard Soderberg Professor of Power Engineering at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). He served as the Department Head of the Department of Mechanical Engineering at MIT from 2013 to 2018. He obtained his PhD degree from the Mechanical Engineering Department at UC Berkeley under the supervision of then UC Berkeley Chancellor Chang-Lin Tien. He was a faculty member at Duke University and UCLA, before joining MIT in 2001. He received an NSF Young Investigator Award, an R&D 100 award, an ASME Heat Transfer Memorial Award, an ASME Frank Kreith Award in Energy, a Nukiyama Memorial Award by the Japan Heat Transfer Society, a World Technology Network Award in Energy, an Eringen medal from the Society of Engineering Science, the Capers and Marion McDonald Award for Excellences in Mentoring and Advising from MIT, a Steven Chu medal from the Asian American Academy of Science and Engineering, and an American Courage Award from Asian American Advancing Justice. He serves on the board of the Asian American Scholar Forum. He is a fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the American Physical Society, The American Society of Mechanical Engineers, and the Guggenheim Foundation. He is a foreign member of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, an academician of Academy Sinica, a fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and a member of the US National Academy of Engineering and a member of the US National Academy of Science.

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract Complex systems can fail in many ways, from cascading failures triggered by random component loss to deliberately targeted attacks. This raises a fundamental question: How can robustness be quantified when a disturbance changes the probability distribution of system outcomes? This talk develops a probabilistic perspective on robustness in which changes in system performance are represented through changes in outcome distributions. Drawing on information theory, these changes are quantified through an entropy-based robustness index that compares system behaviour before and after a disturbance. The index builds on concepts and methods from system reliability and complements conventional reliability and risk measures by characterizing how system behaviour changes when disrupted. About the Speaker Alex Sixie Cao is an Assistant Professor in the School of Civil and Environmental Engineering at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, where he leads the Risk and Infrastructure Systems Lab. His work spans impact loading and structural mechanics, mechanical and probabilistic modelling of progressive collapse and cascading failures, quantitative measures of robustness, and risk-informed decision-making. Alex also studies how structural safety objectives and infrastructure decisions should evolve under long-term environmental and societal change, including climate change. He received his doctorate from ETH Zurich, where his research focused on modelling progressive collapse in buildings, and his MSc in Structural Engineering from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology. Before joining NTU, he was a postdoctoral researcher at Empa and ETH Zurich, working across structural mechanics, system reliability, and robustness. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Dr. Taeyoung Kim is an associate professor at Clarkson University, holding a joint appointment in the Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering and the Institute for a Sustainable Environment. He joined the faculty as an assistant professor in 2018 and was promoted to associate professor in 2025. Currently, Dr. Kim is a visiting fellow at Princeton University, collaborating with Dr. Ryan Kingsbury. Prior to joining Clarkson, he was a postdoctoral scholar in Civil and Environmental Engineering at Penn State. He earned his B.S. and Ph.D. degrees in Chemical and Biological Engineering from Seoul National University. Abstract: Electrochemical separations offer a compelling paradigm for process intensification by directly using electrons to drive separations, overcoming the key challenges of conventional separation technologies that rely heavily on chemicals, thermal energy, or high pressures. Electrochemical energy devices represent some of the most successful electron-driven systems that we benefit from in everyday life, and understanding their fundamental mechanisms allows these operating principles to be effectively leveraged for environmental applications. This talk highlights our efforts in adapting core principles from electrochemical energy devices—such as supercapacitors, batteries, and fuel cells—to design innovative electrochemical separation processes. Leveraging redox chemistries and ion-exchange membranes, these processes offer key advantages including high target selectivity, modularity, and direct integration with renewable electricity. This talk will demonstrate their successful application in brackish water desalination, brine management, and selective resource recovery. Finally, key takeaways learned from operational and scientific challenges will be discussed alongside future steps toward establishing electrochemical separations as a robust, scalable platform for environmental sustainability. Lunch will be served at noon.

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Dr. Mark Falinski is a Senior Manager at the World Resources Institute’s Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition. His work examines how U.S. and global energy systems can navigate growing electricity demand while becoming cleaner, more reliable, and more affordable. His current work spans a range of energy transition issues, with a particular focus on leading research and congressional engagement around the rapid growth of data centers and their implications for energy, water, industrial decarbonization, communities, and sustainability. Mark holds a B.S. in Chemical Engineering from the University at Buffalo and a Ph.D. in Environmental Engineering from Yale University’s Center for Green Chemistry and Green Engineering. He later conducted postdoctoral research in Professor Jason Ren’s Water & Energy Technologies Lab at Princeton University. He has also led research at a sustainability startup and worked as a Climate and Sustainability Consultant at Boston Consulting Group, where his work addressed sustainable finance, circularity strategy, and material supply chains for the energy transition. Mark has most recently served as a AAAS Climate and Energy Fellow in Congress for U.S. Representative Sean Casten of Illinois. There, he developed federal legislation on clean energy deployment, electric grid regulation, and data center impacts, while also working on environmental policy, sustainable finance, water, and climate risk issues. Today, he draws on both his technical and policy backgrounds to examine complex energy and sustainability challenges. His work engages Congress, utilities, hyperscalers, technology providers, and environmental NGOs, with a focus on making complex technical and policy issues accessible to policymakers and their staff, identifying areas of common ground across groups with differing priorities, and helping advance practical solutions. ENE/CEE Lecture Highlights: Overview of the energy, water, and other emerging environmental problems stemming from AI data centers The known and unknown technical and policy constraints to clean, affordable, reliable outcomes from data center development (and how different actors are considering those constraints) Technical and policy solutions to those challenges, including the resource recovery options that will need to be part of the picture (waste heat, e-waste, water reuse) and what is needed to scale the needed clean energy and grid technologies from a policy and technological perspective

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Alessandro Vespignani Sternberg Family Distinguished Professor Northeastern University Abstract : Concepts developed to describe spreading processes on networks, including the role of heterogeneous connectivity, have provided the foundation for a new generation of mechanistic models. Built on empirical mobility and contact networks, these models capture the multi-scale nature of contagion in real populations. These methodological and data integration advances enabled epidemic modeling to evolve into a public-service activity, generating forecasts and analytics that inform policy in real time. The same framework supports the design of surveillance systems, such as global aircraft-based wastewater monitoring, where the structure of the air-transportation network becomes an asset for early detection. The lecture will discuss this trajectory and why consolidating these capabilities is now a central requirement of pandemic preparedness beyond emergency response. Bio : Alessandro Vespignani is the Sternberg Family Distinguished University Professor at Northeastern University, where he founded and directs the Network Science Institute. His research focuses on the modeling of contagion processes in complex networks, from the spread of infectious diseases to the diffusion of information. He leads EPISTORM, a national center for epidemic emergency analytics funded by the U.S. CDC. He is elected Fellow of the APS, the Network Science Society, and the AAAS. His awards include the Euler Award and the EPS Statistical and Nonlinear Physics Prize.

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Lei Zhao is an Associate Professor of Civil and Environmental Engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. His research focuses on the interactions between the climate system and the built environment. He integrates theory, Earth system modeling, remote sensing, and AI/ML to advance the understanding and prediction of urban climate, extremes and their impacts on cities, and to develop strategies for urban resilience and adaptation. He is a Fellow of the American Geophysical Union (AGU) and a recipient of the AGU James B. Macelwane Medal (2025), the Timothy Oke Award from the International Association for Urban Climate (2023), the AGU Global Environmental Change Early Career Award (2023), and the NSF CAREER Award (2021). He was also named a Clarivate Highly Cited Researcher in 2025. He received his Ph.D. in atmospheric physics from Yale University and B.S. from Nanjing University and was a postdoctoral fellow at Princeton University before joining UIUC. Abstract: Urbanization represents one of the most significant anthropogenic changes to the Earth’s surface, with profound climatic effects across scales. Many of the most pressing climate risks, including heat stress, water scarcity, extreme precipitation, and energy insecurity, are either rooted in or exacerbated by the unique built environment. Absent measures to ameliorate them, these risks will significantly intensify due to the rapid urban development coupled with climate change. An additional ~2.5 billion people are projected to reside in urban areas by year 2050. This unprecedented transformation poses immense risks to cities and their residents, but also an historic, time-sensitive opportunity to reshape how cities contribute to sustainability and climate resilience. Addressing this grand challenge, however, requires novel modeling frameworks that better resolve urban effects and their complex two-way interactions with climate across spatiotemporal scales, both for improved scientific understanding of cities and for planning effective resilient strategies. Recent advances in AI/ML, satellite remote sensing, high-resolution urban-resolving Earth system modeling, and advanced computing have enabled development of many of these advanced tools and opened up promising opportunities. In this talk, I will present how urban-resolving Earth system modeling, satellite remote sensing, AI/ML-based hybrid approaches, and advanced computing address longstanding challenges in urban climate science, from closing modeling and data gaps to projecting urban climate extremes and impacts, and how they can inform strategies for building resilient cities in a warming world.

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Patrick Brewick is currently an Assistant Professor in the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering & Earth Sciences at the University of Notre Dame. Dr. Brewick earned his B.S. (2009) in Civil Engineering from the University of Notre Dame and M.S. (2010) and Ph.D. (2014) in Civil Engineering and Engineering Mechanics from Columbia University. After his Ph.D., Dr. Brewick spent two years as a Viterbi Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of Southern California in the Sonny Astani Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering. Following his postdoc, Dr. Brewick spent several years as a Research Scientist in the Materials Science and Technology Division of the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory before joining the University of Notre Dame. Abstract: Engineers rely upon models every day in a variety of contexts, up to an including the digital twins that are emerging as an increasingly essential tool for designing, maintaining, and monitoring infrastructure. Unfortunately, as the aphorism goes, “all models are wrong.” Engineers should not lose hope, though, because models can still become useful when they are informed by measurements and observations. In this context, the importance of properly leveraging experimental data for informed model selection and careful parameter estimation becomes apparent. However, the inherent and ubiquitous presence of structural and parametric uncertainties add significant layers of complexity to these modeling tasks, necessitating the use of uncertainty quantification tools such as Bayesian inference. This presentation will discuss various projects located at this nexus of data, modeling, mechanics, and uncertainty. Applications include using novel response data from distributed fiber optics for modal identification, selecting the most probable nonlinear models for seismic isolation systems, and implementing hierarchical Bayesian approaches for calibrating hysteretic models based on experimental data from full-scale shake table testing. Lunch will be served at noon.
